diagrams.title: Systemic Evaluation for a Patient With CLE
diagrams.subtitle: A risk-proportionate baseline and follow-up pathway

items.label: Subtype, distribution, activity, damage, and onset
items.detail: ACLE, SCLE, generalized DLE, childhood DLE, vasculitic lesions, and nonscarring alopecia generally justify a lower threshold for systemic evaluation than a single localized DLE plaque.

items.label: Joint, renal, hematologic, neurologic, cardiopulmonary, thrombotic, mucosal and constitutional review
Medication, supplement, smoking, UV, pregnancy, and infection history
items.detail: New SCLE requires a detailed medication timeline.

items.label: CBC with differential; creatinine/eGFR; liver profile as indicated
Urinalysis with sediment; quantify protein if abnormal
ANA (preferably IF), anti-dsDNA, C3/C4; ENA and antiphospholipid tests when phenotype warrants
items.detail: Do not diagnose or treat SLE based on an isolated positive ANA.

items.label: Proteinuria, hematuria/casts, or renal dysfunction → urgent rheumatology/nephrology pathway
Hemolysis or significant cytopenia → confirm cause and assess active SLE, drug toxicity, infection, or marrow disease
Seizure, psychosis, focal deficit, thrombosis, or severe serositis → emergency organ-specific evaluation
Frequency follows subtype, symptoms, prior abnormalities, treatment, and pregnancy status
items.detail: Classification criteria are research tools that can organize findings but do not replace clinical diagnosis.

citations.quote: Garg, Merola, and Fitzpatrick (eds.). Interdisciplinary Approaches to Overlap Disorders in Dermatology & Rheumatology. Springer, 2022.
EULAR 2023 recommendations emphasize hydroxychloroquine, glucocorticoid minimization, organ-directed immunosuppression, and biologic options in SLE.

diagrams.title: New or Worsening SCLE: Is It Drug-Induced?
diagrams.subtitle: A medication-timeline workflow

steps.prompt: Annular/polycyclic or papulosquamous photodistributed eruption compatible with SCLE?

steps.detail: Dermatomyositis, psoriasis, tinea, polymorphous light eruption, photoallergic/phototoxic dermatitis, drug exanthem, and CTCL can mimic SCLE.

steps.prompt: Build a complete medication and supplement timeline
steps.detail: Include recent starts, dose changes, intermittent drugs, and agents discontinued weeks to months earlier. Common implicated classes include proton-pump inhibitors, thiazides/other antihypertensives, terbinafine, TNF inhibitors, anticonvulsants, and others.

steps.prompt: New widespread disease, older onset, or close temporal relation to a plausible agent?
When clinically safe, coordinate withdrawal/substitution of the suspected agent
steps.detail: Do not stop an essential therapy without the prescribing clinician. Treat active skin disease concurrently; improvement may take weeks to months.

steps.prompt: Anti-Ro/SSA, lupus symptoms, or persistent disease after withdrawal?
Evaluate for idiopathic CLE/SLE and treat by severity
steps.detail: Drug-induced and idiopathic SCLE can share anti-Ro positivity and histology; persistence does not automatically exclude a drug contribution.

steps.prompt: Document response and reconsider competing diagnoses
steps.detail: Re-biopsy or pursue patch/photopatch testing when morphology or course is discordant.

diagrams.title: CLE Treatment by Phenotype and Risk
diagrams.subtitle: Escalate for active scarring disease, extent, symptoms, or systemic involvement

foundation.text: Broad-spectrum UV protection, protective clothing, smoking cessation; site-appropriate topical corticosteroid or calcineurin inhibitor.

systemic.text: Hydroxychloroquine if persistent, recurrent, symptomatic, or too extensive for local therapy.

refractory.text: Recheck diagnosis, drug triggers, UV exposure, adherence, and antimalarial exposure before adding another systemic agent.

rows.name: DLE / scarring scalp or face disease

foundation.text: Treat active border early; potent topical or intralesional corticosteroid where appropriate; photograph and track activity vs scar.

systemic.text: Hydroxychloroquine is usual first systemic therapy; add/transition to methotrexate or mycophenolate when disease remains active or progressive.

refractory.text: Selected retinoid, dapsone, thalidomide/lenalidomide, or other specialist therapy; biopsy changing hypertrophic/nonhealing lesions to exclude SCC.

foundation.text: Deep biopsy; analgesia and damage documentation; local therapy alone is often insufficient.

systemic.text: Antimalarial plus a steroid-sparing agent selected by severity and systemic phenotype; a short glucocorticoid bridge may be needed.

refractory.text: Reassess for lymphoma mimic and active SLE; contour reconstruction should wait until inflammation is inactive.

foundation.text: Continue skin-directed care and photoprotection while defining the organ-threatening domain.

systemic.text: Hydroxychloroquine unless contraindicated; minimize glucocorticoid exposure; select immunosuppressive therapy to control the dominant systemic organ.

refractory.text: Anifrolumab, belimumab, rituximab, cyclophosphamide, or other therapy may be appropriate depending on organ involvement and prior response.
